content: Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen (PCNA) is a protein that functions as a processivity factor for DNA polymerase delta in eukaryotic cells. It achieves this by forming a ring-like structure that encircles the DNA, creating a stable topological link to the genome. This structural feature classifies PCNA as a DNA clamp. The protein encoded by the PCNA gene is localized in the nucleus and serves as a cofactor for DNA polymerase delta. It functions as a homotrimer, enhancing the processivity of leading strand synthesis during DNA replication. When DNA damage occurs, PCNA undergoes ubiquitination and participates in the RAD6-dependent DNA repair pathway. Two transcript variants encoding the same PCNA protein have been identified. Additionally, pseudogenes of PCNA have been located on chromosome 4 and the X chromosome. PCNA was initially discovered as an antigen expressed in the nuclei of cells during the DNA synthesis phase of the cell cycle. A partial sequence of the protein was determined, which facilitated the isolation of a complementary DNA (cDNA) clone. PCNA plays a critical role in anchoring DNA polymerase delta to the DNA template. This anchoring is mediated by replication factor C (RFC), a heteropentameric complex belonging to the AAA+ family of ATPases. The expression of PCNA is regulated by complexes containing the E2F transcription factor. In addition to its role in DNA replication, PCNA is essential for DNA repair processes. DNA polymerase delta, which is involved in the resynthesis of excised DNA strands during repair, relies on PCNA for its function. Furthermore, PCNA is implicated in the transition to DNA damage bypass mechanisms, such as translesion synthesis, which allows replication to proceed despite the presence of DNA lesions.
